11.2 Abelian Groups of prime power order Before we cover the classification of abelian groups, we must first understand direct products and abelian groups whose order is a prime power. Proposition 11.2.1. Let 𝐶𝑛 and 𝐶𝑚 be finite cyclic groups such that gcd(𝑚, 𝑛) = 1. Then 𝐶𝑛 × 𝐶𝑚 ≅ 𝐶𝑛𝑚. Proof. Let 𝑚, 𝑛 ∈ ℕ be such that gcd(𝑚, 𝑛) = 1. The group 𝐶𝑛𝑚 is generated by a single element 𝜌 whose order is 𝑛𝑚. Now 𝐶𝑛𝑚 is cyclic and so it is abelian. Hence every subgroup of 𝐶𝑛𝑚 is normal. Let 𝐺 = ⟨𝜌𝑚⟩ ≤ 𝐶𝑛𝑚 and 𝐻 = ⟨𝜌𝑛⟩ ≤ 𝐶𝑛𝑚. Since 𝑜(𝜌𝑚) = 𝑛 and 𝑜(𝜌𝑛) = 𝑚 we have 𝐺 ≅ 𝐶𝑛 and 𝐻 ≅ 𝐶𝑚. Every subgroup of 𝐶𝑛𝑚 is normal. Therefore 𝐺⊴𝐶𝑛𝑚 and 𝐻 ⊴𝐶𝑛𝑚. Moreover, if 𝜌𝑘 ∈ 𝐺∩𝐻, then 𝑘 must be a multiple of 𝑚 and a multiple of 𝑛, which implies that 𝜌𝑘 = 𝑒. Hence 𝐺 ∩ 𝐻 = ⟨𝑒⟩. Hence 𝐺𝐻 is an internal direct product, so by Theorem 11.1.3, 𝐺𝐻 ≅ 𝐺 × 𝐻 ≅ 𝐶𝑛 × 𝐶𝑚. Finally, we note that since 𝐺𝐻 ≅ 𝐶𝑛 × 𝐶𝑚, we have |𝐺𝐻| = 𝑛𝑚. Moreover, 𝐺𝐻 ≤ 𝐶𝑛𝑚 and |𝐶𝑛𝑚| = 𝑛𝑚. Therefore 𝐺𝐻 = 𝐶𝑛𝑚. Hence 𝐶𝑛𝑚 ≅ 𝐶𝑛 × 𝐶𝑚. Proposition 11.2.2. Let 𝐶𝑛 and 𝐶𝑚 be finite cyclic groups such that gcd(𝑚, 𝑛) ≠ 1. Then 𝐶𝑛 × 𝐶𝑚 ≇ 𝐶𝑛𝑚. Proof. Suppose, for a contradiction, that 𝜃 ∶ 𝐶𝑛𝑚 → 𝐶𝑛 × 𝐶𝑚 is an isomorphism. Now 𝐶𝑛𝑚 is cyclic, so 𝐶𝑛𝑚 = ⟨𝑔⟩ for some element 𝑔 of order 𝑛𝑚. Let 𝜃(𝑔) = (𝑎, 𝑏), for some 𝑎 ∈ 𝐶𝑛 and 𝑏 ∈ 𝐶𝑚. Since 𝜃 is an isomorphism, it must be the case that 𝑜((𝑎, 𝑏)) = 𝑜(𝑔) = 𝑛𝑚. Let 𝑑 = gcd(𝑚, 𝑛) > 1, and write 𝑚 = 𝑟𝑑 and 𝑛 = 𝑠𝑑. Since 𝑑 > 1 we have that 𝑚𝑠 < 𝑚𝑛. Now (𝑎, 𝑏)𝑚𝑠 = (𝑎𝑟𝑑𝑠, 𝑏𝑟𝑑𝑠) = ((𝑎𝑠𝑑)𝑟, (𝑏𝑟𝑑)𝑠) = ((𝑎𝑛)𝑟, (𝑏𝑚)𝑠) = (𝑒, 𝑒). Thus, 𝑜((𝑎, 𝑏)) ≤ 𝑚𝑠 < 𝑛𝑚. A contradiction. Example 11.2.3. Consider the following examples. • 𝐶80 = 𝐶24⋅5 ≅ 𝐶24 × 𝐶5 (By Proposition 0.1.1) • 𝐶7 × 𝐶52 ≅ 𝐶7⋅52 = 𝐶175 (By Proposition 0.1.1) • 𝐶2 × 𝐶2 ≇ 𝐶4 (By Proposition 0.1.2) • 𝐶2 × 𝐶22 × 𝐶23 and 𝐶23 × 𝐶23 and 𝐶26 are all nonisomorphic. (By Proposition 0.1.2) We know the structure of all finite abelian 𝑝-groups. Theorem 11.2.4. Let 𝑝 be a prime and let 𝐺 be a finite abelian group of order 𝑝𝑛. Then there are natural numbers 𝑒1, 𝑒2, … , 𝑒𝑡 such that 𝐺 is isomorphic to a direct product 𝐶𝑝𝑒1 × 𝐶𝑝𝑒2 × ⋯ × 𝐶𝑝𝑒𝑡 , where 𝑝𝑒1𝑝𝑒2 ⋯ 𝑝𝑒𝑡 = 𝑝𝑛, and this factorisation is unique up to reordering of the factors. 101
